newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra scrambles on secret Pacific report fallout.
newsitem.headline: Canberra scrambles on secret Pacific report fallout.

text.p: Australia on Sunday moved to limit the diplomatic fallout from the release of a scathing report on its South Pacific neighbours, as officials began a probe into how the top secret paper was left on a hotel table.

Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith, one of the government's top officials, stressed the report -- highly critical of regional economies and the personal habits of their economic ministers -- was not the government's view.
"These things happen in politics but it's not the view of the government," Reith said in a television interview.
"We place an important priority on good relations with the Pacific Islands."
Reith said comments in the 93-page report -- marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian Eyes Only -- were nowhere near as damaging as past bungles by the former Labor government.

"Who can forget the famous 'recalcitrant' comment from (former prime minister) Paul Keating (about Malaysian leader Mahathir Mohamad) that did such tremendous damage to Australia's economic relations with one of its biggest partners?" he said.
That 1993 row chilled relations between Canberra and Kuala Lumpur and at its height threatened millions of dollars in trade.
But the Pacific countries of Nauru and the Cook Islands -- among those most heavily criticised -- have condemned the report as insulting and wrong.
Treasury officials on Sunday began inquiries into how such a sensitive document -- AUSTEO ranks far higher than top secret -- was left in a public place.
The Cook Islands said on Saturday the report was offensive and contained "significant inaccuracies" and Australia's Labor opposition labelled it a major diplomatic blunder.
"I cannot recall a document as systematically offensive ever being written while I was foreign minister," acting opposition leader and former foreign minister Gareth Evans.

Nauru President Kinza Clodumar said in a statement that the document was "most insulting and patronising" to the Nauru government. "I am sure they are feeling very hurt -- it's a most dreadful report," Clodumar said.
"As reported, the document sounded as though it was heavily laced with rumour and scuttlebutt, rather than an attempt to provide sound analytical advice," he said.

The paper was prepared jointly by the treasury and the foreign affairs department for Treasurer Peter Costello as a briefing for a summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the tropical resort town of Cairns.
It was left on a table in a public area at the summit where it was obtained by Reuters.

New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters -- labelled a loose cannon and an opportunist in the briefing -- said on Sunday he document should not upset Canberra-Wellington relations.
Peters told TV1 television that the papers would be deeply embarrassing for Canberra "but we are not going to pay any attention to that or it will upset our relations with Australia".
A spokesman for Peters said the paper was merely the work of "an ignorant bureaucrat".
